extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reading MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent claims under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice/Mayo framework), including when to use a streamlined analysis and how to formulate and support eligibility rejections. Targets how examiners should identify judicial exceptions and assess whether additional claim elements amount to 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use / technological environment limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely indicate a field of use or technological environment in which to apply a judicial exception (e.g., limiting administration of a drug to a certain patient population, limiting an abstract idea to use on the Internet or in a telephone network).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have described such limitations as mere field-of-use/technological-environment restrictions that do not add an inventive concept because they lack integration into the claim as a whole. Examples (i–x) are provided (Mayo/Prometheus; Bilski; Flook; FairWarning; Intellectual Ventures; Electric Power Group; Genetic Techs.; Ultramercial; buySAFE). Examiners should consider the terms 'technological environment' and 'field of use' interchangeable and note overlap with Step 2B considerations (insignificant extra-solution activity per MPEP § 2106.05(g)). For claim limitations that generally link the exception to a particular environment, examiners should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim (e.g., employing well-known computer functions to execute an abstract idea is insufficient).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of additional elements into the claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: A common feature of many non-meaningful claim limitations is an absence of integration into the claim as a whole; integrated limitations act in concert to transform the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Diehr/Flook comparison: Diehr's claim recited specific, interrelated limitations (monitoring elapsed time, constantly measuring temperature, repetitively calculating cure time and automatically opening the press) that together transformed raw material and integrated the mathematical equation into an improved process; Flook's catalytic conversion limitation was merely incidental and did not alter how the claimed steps were performed. Examiners should assess whether additional elements are integrated (meaningfully limit application of the exception) or merely incidental/token additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis (Pathway A)
rubrics_metrics.description: A streamlined eligibility analysis may be used when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (e.g., claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The streamlined (Pathway A) result must be the same as the full analysis; it is not a way to avoid an ineligibility finding. If there is doubt whether the applicant is effectively seeking coverage for the exception itself, perform the full Alice/Mayo analysis. The record may simply reflect eligibility by absence of a §101 rejection or include clarifying remarks. If viewed as a whole the claim's eligibility is self-evident, the claim is eligible at Pathway A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility is self-evident (criteria for using Pathway A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that clearly do not seek to tie up a judicial exception such that others cannot practice it, and thus need not proceed through the full analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: complex manufactured industrial products or processes that recite meaningful limitations (e.g., robotic arm assembly with control system using mathematical relationships), artificial hip prosthesis coated with naturally occurring mineral, or claims with merely ancillary nature-based components (cellphone with gold contact). If claims are a close call, conduct full analysis. Claims that do not qualify under Step 2B are not suitable for streamlined analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear improvement to technology or computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to clear improvements to technology or computer functionality may not be abstract and therefore may avoid full eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Enfish (self-referential table), McRO (automatic lip sync & facial expression animation) as examples where claims viewed as a whole showed a clear improvement. If improvement is clear, examiner may reasonably find eligibility at Pathway A or Step 2A; if a 'close call' proceed to Step 2B. See MPEP § 2106.05 for considerations on improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating and supporting rejections for lack of subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rejections must be based on substantive law under 35 U.S.C. §101 as interpreted by case law; guidance/training materials do not themselves serve as the basis for a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before concluding whether claimed invention is patent-eligible, review the record as a whole (specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law, prior art) and evaluate each claim on its own merits. If it's more likely than not that a claim fails eligibility (Step 1:NO and/or Step 2B:NO), formulate an appropriate rejection under Step 1 and/or Step 2B that sets forth a prima facie case of ineligibility. The examiner bears the initial burden to explain clearly and specifically why a claim is ineligible so the applicant can respond effectively. When maintaining a rejection after applicant's response, provide a rebuttal in the next Office action as appropriate (MPEP § 2106.07(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: When making a rejection, identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rejection must point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why those limitations set forth an exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon, product of nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For abstract ideas, identify the abstract idea as recited in the claim and explain why it corresponds to concepts courts have identified as abstract (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2)); citing a supportive court decision is best practice. For laws of nature/natural phenomena, identify the law/phenomenon as recited and provide a reasoned rationale. For product of nature, identify the product and explain why it does not have markedly different characteristics from its natural counterpart. Sample explanations are provided (e.g., claim reciting sorting information by X corresponds to abstract ideas in Digitech/Content Extraction; claim reciting correlation of X is a law of nature because it describes a natural bodily consequence). Avoid relying on non-precedential decisions unless facts uniquely match.

rubrics_metrics.name: When making a rejection, explain why additional claim elements do not result in significantly more than the judicial exception (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the exception and explain why they do not add 'significantly more' to the exception, addressing elements individually and in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why additional elements, taken individually and as a combination, fail to amount to significantly more. Note that a new combination of well-known steps can be patent eligible (Diamond v. Diehr); therefore carefully consider whether the combination meaningfully limits the judicial exception. When an examiner concludes elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the rejection should explain why courts or those in the field would so recognize them. See MPEP § 2106.05 for a listing of considerations courts have found to qualify or not qualify as significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reasoned rationale when concluding elements are well-understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: If examiner concludes particular claim elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities in the relevant field, the rejection must include an explanation supporting that conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rejection should explain why the courts have recognized, or those in the field would recognize, the additional elements as well-understood, routine, conventional. Provide a reasoned explanation (not conclusory) to support the prima facie finding that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate subject matter eligibility on a claim-by-claim basis; claims do not automatically rise or fall with similar claims in an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an independent claim is ineligible, dependent claims may be eligible because they add limitations amounting to significantly more than the judicial exception in the independent claim. Consider the record as a whole (specification, prosecution history, prior art, case law) for each claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and apply product-of-nature/markedly-different-characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim recites a product of nature, the rejection should identify that exception and explain why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart and provide a reasoned rationale showing there is no marked difference in structure, function, or other properties as supported by the record. Sample language: 'X is a nature-based product ... there is no indication in the record that isolation of X has resulted in a marked difference ... X is a product of nature exception.' See MPEP § 2106.04(b)/(c) for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite appropriate precedent and tie rejection to facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should cite appropriate court decisions that support identification of the exception and the eligibility conclusion, and ensure citations are reasonably tied to the facts of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing a supportive decision is best practice and advances prosecution. Examiners should be familiar with any cited decision to avoid relying on language taken out of context. Avoid reliance on non-precedential decisions unless the facts uniquely match those decisions. A chart of court decisions is available on the USPTO website for reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution — examine all other patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether a §101 rejection is made, a complete examination should be made for every claim under other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, utility, inventorship, double patenting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action. Do not omit consideration of other grounds merely because a §101 issue is present.
